title: Excedrin and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Liver, Stomach, and Caffeine Risks
excerpt: Can you take Excedrin after drinking? How its acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine each interact with alcohol, how long to wait for a hangover headache, and warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you take Excedrin after drinking? How its acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine interact with alcohol, how long to wait, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Excedrin is three drugs in one pill, and each of them interacts with alcohol in a different way. The acetaminophen adds work for your liver, the aspirin raises the chance of stomach bleeding, and the caffeine can make you feel more sober than you are. For most healthy adults, a single labeled dose of Excedrin the morning after a few drinks, taken with food once the alcohol has cleared, is unlikely to cause serious harm. Taking it while you're still drinking, taking it to "prevent" a hangover, taking more than the label allows, or using it regularly when you drink most days is where the real risk sits.

**The quick rules:** Don't take Excedrin before or during drinking. Wait until you're sober, eat something, and take one labeled dose with a full glass of water. Don't stack it with Tylenol, NyQuil, DayQuil, or any other product that contains acetaminophen, and don't stack it with ibuprofen or naproxen. If you have 3 or more drinks every day, have a history of stomach ulcers or bleeding, take a blood thinner, or have liver disease, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using Excedrin at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the warnings printed on Excedrin's US label. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Get medical help right away if** you may have taken more than the labeled dose, you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, you pass black or bloody stools, you feel faint, or you notice pain under your right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine after taking Excedrin. In the US, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222**. In an emergency, call 911.

## What's Actually in Excedrin?

Most people think of Excedrin as "the strong headache pill." It earns that reputation by combining three ingredients that each help with pain in a different way. The standard US formulas look like this:

| Product | Acetaminophen | Aspirin | Caffeine | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Excedrin Extra Strength | 250 mg | 250 mg | 65 mg | none |
| Excedrin Migraine | 250 mg | 250 mg | 65 mg | none |
| Excedrin Tension Headache | 500 mg | none | 65 mg | none |
| Excedrin PM Headache | 250 mg | 250 mg | none | diphenhydramine (a sleep aid) |

A few things jump out:

- **Excedrin Extra Strength and Excedrin Migraine contain the same ingredients in the same amounts.** The difference is the labeling and directions, not the pill. The migraine label is written for migraine attacks and limits use more tightly.
- **A typical dose is two caplets.** That means 500 mg of acetaminophen, 500 mg of aspirin, and 130 mg of caffeine at once. That's about the caffeine in a strong cup of coffee.
- **Not every Excedrin has aspirin, and not every Excedrin has caffeine.** Tension Headache drops the aspirin, and PM Headache swaps caffeine for a sedating antihistamine. That changes how each one interacts with alcohol, so always read the box you actually have.

Formulas can change and vary by country, so check the Drug Facts panel on your package. Everything below refers to the standard US products.

## Why Each Ingredient Clashes With Alcohol

The reason Excedrin and alcohol deserve more caution than a single-ingredient painkiller is that you get three separate interactions stacked together. Here's each one in plain words.

### 1. Acetaminophen: extra load on the liver

Acetaminophen is the same drug that's in Tylenol. Your liver clears most of each dose safely, but a small share is turned into a toxic by-product called NAPQI. Your liver neutralizes NAPQI with an antioxidant called glutathione. Trouble starts when NAPQI is produced faster than glutathione can clean it up.

Regular heavy drinking pushes on both sides of that balance. It ramps up the liver enzyme (CYP2E1) that makes NAPQI, and it tends to lower glutathione stores, especially when someone isn't eating well. That's why the acetaminophen warning on every Excedrin box says severe liver damage may occur if you take more than the label allows, take it with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product.

The good news is that the amount of acetaminophen in a normal Excedrin dose (500 mg) is modest, about the same as one Extra Strength Tylenol caplet. The real-world danger is less about one dose and more about **doubling up without realizing it**. If you take Excedrin for the headache, NyQuil to sleep, and a Tylenol later because the headache came back, the acetaminophen adds up fast. Our full guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers the liver chemistry, safe daily ceilings, and warning signs in more detail.

### 2. Aspirin: stomach irritation and bleeding risk

Aspirin is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), in the same broad family as ibuprofen and naproxen. It works by blocking enzymes called COX-1 and COX-2, which make prostaglandins. Some prostaglandins drive pain and inflammation, which is why aspirin helps a headache. Others protect your stomach lining by keeping its mucus layer thick and its blood flow healthy. When aspirin turns those protective prostaglandins down, the stomach lining becomes easier to injure.

Alcohol irritates the same lining directly. Put the two together and you have two separate insults landing on the same tissue, often on an empty stomach after a night out. That's the reason the Excedrin label carries a stomach bleeding warning that specifically calls out people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product, along with people over 60, people with a history of ulcers or bleeding, and people taking blood thinners or steroids.

Aspirin has a second effect that matters here. It blocks platelets, the blood cells that start a clot, and it does so **permanently for the life of each platelet**, which is roughly 7 to 10 days. That's why aspirin is used in low doses for heart protection. It also means that if something does start bleeding in your stomach, it may not stop as easily. Unlike ibuprofen or naproxen, whose effect on platelets wears off as the drug leaves your body, aspirin's effect lingers until your body makes new platelets.

There's one more, less well-known interaction. A small human study published in *JAMA* in 1990 (Roine and colleagues) found that taking aspirin an hour before drinking raised blood alcohol levels compared with drinking alone. The proposed explanation is that aspirin reduces the activity of an alcohol-processing enzyme in the stomach lining, so more alcohol reaches your bloodstream. It was a small study and the effect size shouldn't be overstated, but it's one more reason not to take aspirin-containing pills before a night out.

If aspirin is the ingredient you're most worried about, our guide to [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol) explains the NSAID side of this in more depth, since naproxen and aspirin share the same stomach warning.

### 3. Caffeine: why it can make you feel more sober than you are

Caffeine is in Excedrin because it genuinely helps. A Cochrane review (Derry and colleagues, 2014) found that adding caffeine to common painkillers like acetaminophen and aspirin gives a small but real boost in the number of people who get good pain relief. It may also help with the type of headache that comes from caffeine withdrawal, which is common the morning after a late night if you skipped your usual coffee.

The problem comes when caffeine and alcohol are in your body at the same time. Caffeine makes you feel more alert. It does **not** lower your blood alcohol level, speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, or restore your reaction time and judgment. Researchers sometimes call this state being "wide awake drunk."

Lab studies by Cecile Marczinski and Mark Fillmore in the mid-2000s showed this clearly: when people drank alcohol mixed with caffeine, they reported feeling less impaired than people who drank the same amount of alcohol alone, but their performance on tests of self-control and quick decisions was still impaired. Concern about this effect was a major reason the US FDA sent warning letters to makers of premixed caffeinated alcoholic drinks in 2010, which led those products to be reformulated.

A two-caplet dose of Excedrin has about 130 mg of caffeine. That's not much compared with an energy drink, but the principle is the same. If you take Excedrin while you're still drinking, or while there's still alcohol in your system, you may feel sharper than you are. That can lead to another drink, a decision to drive, or underestimating how much you've had. Feeling awake is not the same as being sober.

Caffeine also has a few smaller downsides during a hangover:

- **It can worsen jitters and anxiety.** If you tend to feel shaky or anxious the day after drinking, a dose of caffeine can make that worse.
- **It can upset your stomach.** Caffeine increases stomach acid, which doesn't help when alcohol and aspirin are already irritating the lining.
- **It can disrupt sleep.** Caffeine's effects can last several hours. Taking Excedrin late in the day after a night out can make it harder to get the recovery sleep you need.

Caffeine is often blamed for dehydration, but in people who drink coffee regularly, the amount in an Excedrin dose has only a mild effect on fluid balance. Alcohol is the bigger driver of fluid loss. Drink water with the pill either way.

## Is It Safe to Take Excedrin After Drinking?

For a healthy adult who drinks occasionally, the answer is usually yes, **with the right timing and dose**. The risks described above add up most in a few specific situations:

- You're still drinking, or still have alcohol in your system.
- You take Excedrin before drinking to try to prevent a hangover.
- You take more than the labeled dose, or take it repeatedly over a long day.
- You combine it with other acetaminophen products, or with ibuprofen, naproxen, or extra aspirin.
- You drink 3 or more drinks most days.
- You have a history of ulcers or stomach bleeding, liver disease, or kidney problems, or you take blood thinners.

If none of those apply to you, a single labeled dose with food the next morning is a reasonable choice for many people. If any of them do apply, talk to a doctor or pharmacist first, and consider a simpler option.

## Hangover Headache Timing: How Long to Wait

There's no official waiting period printed on the Excedrin label, so the guidance below is common-sense practice rather than a rule. The goal is simple: let the alcohol clear before you add three drugs on top of it.

**1. Wait until you're sober.** Your body clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults, though this varies with body size, sex, food, and genetics. After a heavy night, there may still be alcohol in your blood when you wake up. A hangover tends to peak as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero, so if you can feel the headache starting while you're still tipsy, that's a sign to wait.

**2. Eat something first.** Food helps protect your stomach lining from the aspirin and slows how quickly the caffeine hits. Toast, crackers, eggs, or a banana are fine. If you can't keep food down, that's a reason to hold off on an aspirin-containing pill entirely.

**3. Drink a full glass of water with it.** Rehydrating helps the headache in its own right, and it's easier on your stomach.

**4. Take one labeled dose, not more.** For Excedrin Extra Strength, the US label directs two caplets with a glass of water, no more than every 6 hours, and no more than 8 caplets in 24 hours. Excedrin Migraine's label is stricter for migraine use: two caplets, and no more than two caplets in 24 hours unless a doctor says otherwise. After drinking, staying well under those limits is the safer choice.

**5. Don't drink again on top of it.** Taking Excedrin in the morning and starting "hair of the dog" drinks at lunch puts you right back into the overlapping-risk situation. Aspirin's effect on platelets lasts days, and acetaminophen and caffeine take several hours to clear.

### How long after taking Excedrin can I drink?

This is the reverse question, and it's worth answering directly. There's no exact safe gap, because the three ingredients leave your body at different speeds:

- **Acetaminophen** is mostly cleared within several hours in a healthy adult.
- **Caffeine** has a half-life of around 5 hours in many adults (meaning half is gone in about 5 hours), though it can be much shorter or longer from person to person.
- **Aspirin's** effect on platelets lasts until your body replaces them, roughly a week or more.

In practice, if you took a single dose of Excedrin in the morning, many people would be well past the acetaminophen and caffeine by evening, but the aspirin's bleeding-related effect will still be there. Keeping evening drinking light, eating with it, and not taking another dose that night is the sensible approach. If you take Excedrin regularly, or take daily aspirin for your heart, ask your doctor how much alcohol is reasonable for you.

## Excedrin Migraine and Alcohol

People often search for this separately, so it's worth saying plainly: **Excedrin Migraine has the same three ingredients as Excedrin Extra Strength**, so all the same interactions apply.

There's an extra wrinkle for people who get migraines. Alcohol, especially red wine, is a commonly reported migraine trigger, and some people get headaches within hours of drinking rather than the next morning. If drinking reliably triggers your migraines, the better long-term fix is to work with a doctor on a migraine plan, not to reach for Excedrin after every drink. Frequent use of any headache medicine, Excedrin included, can also lead to **medication overuse headache**, where the pills themselves start causing more frequent headaches. The Excedrin Migraine label tells you to see a doctor if your headaches are getting worse or more frequent.

## Excedrin Tension Headache and Excedrin PM With Alcohol

Because these two products have different ingredients, they interact with alcohol differently.

**Excedrin Tension Headache** has no aspirin, just acetaminophen and caffeine. That removes the stomach bleeding concern from aspirin, but it doubles the acetaminophen per dose (1,000 mg in two caplets, the same as two Extra Strength Tylenol). So the liver warning matters more, and you should be especially careful not to combine it with other acetaminophen products after drinking. The caffeine concerns are the same as above.

**Excedrin PM Headache** replaces caffeine with diphenhydramine, the sedating antihistamine found in Benadryl and many "PM" sleep products. Alcohol and diphenhydramine both slow down your brain, and the combination can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and trouble breathing in rare cases at high doses. The label warns against using it with alcohol and against driving. **Do not take Excedrin PM after drinking to help you sleep.** It's one of the riskier ways to combine a headache pill with alcohol, especially for older adults.

## The Hidden Double-Dosing Problem

The single biggest practical risk with Excedrin after a night out isn't any one ingredient. It's taking the same ingredient twice from different products without noticing. Common combinations to watch for:

- **Excedrin plus Tylenol.** Both contain acetaminophen.
- **Excedrin plus NyQuil, DayQuil, or other cold and flu products.** Many contain acetaminophen. If you're hungover and also have a cold, read every label. Our guide to [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol) covers this in detail.
- **Excedrin plus Advil, Motrin, or Aleve.** Ibuprofen and naproxen add to aspirin's stomach risk.
- **Excedrin plus Alka-Seltzer (original).** The original Alka-Seltzer contains aspirin.
- **Excedrin plus Pepto-Bismol.** Bismuth subsalicylate is chemically related to aspirin, and its label warns people who are allergic to aspirin or taking other salicylates. See our [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol) guide.
- **Excedrin plus daily low-dose aspirin.** If you already take aspirin for your heart, ask your doctor before adding Excedrin.
- **Excedrin plus coffee and energy drinks.** The label tells you to limit caffeine from other sources, because too much can cause nervousness, irritability, sleeplessness, and a fast heartbeat.

A good habit: before you take anything the morning after drinking, line up every product you've taken in the last 24 hours and read the "Active ingredients" line on each one.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who take one dose of Excedrin after a night out feel nothing unusual. But because this pill touches both the stomach and the liver, it's worth knowing what a problem looks like.

**Signs of stomach bleeding (from aspirin and alcohol):**

- Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
- Black, sticky, or bloody stools
- Stomach pain that doesn't go away
- Feeling faint, dizzy, or unusually weak

**Signs of liver trouble (from acetaminophen and alcohol):**

- Nausea, vomiting, sweating, or loss of appetite that doesn't improve as the hangover fades
- Pain under the right ribs
- Yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine
- Confusion or unusual drowsiness

Early liver injury can feel a lot like a bad hangover, which is what makes it easy to miss. If there's any chance you took more acetaminophen than the label allows, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) right away, even if you feel fine. The hospital antidote works best when it's given early.

**Signs of too much caffeine:**

- Racing or pounding heartbeat
- Shakiness, severe anxiety, or chest discomfort

Chest pain, fainting, or trouble breathing are always reasons to call 911.

## Who Should Avoid Excedrin With Alcohol Entirely

Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using Excedrin at all, and especially around drinking, if you:

- Have 3 or more alcoholic drinks most days
- Have liver disease, or have been told your liver enzymes are high
- Have had a stomach ulcer, stomach bleeding, or a bleeding disorder
- Take a blood thinner (such as warfarin or a newer anticoagulant), a steroid, or daily aspirin
- Take an SSRI antidepressant, which can also add to bleeding risk
- Have kidney disease, high blood pressure, heart disease, or asthma that flares with aspirin or NSAIDs
- Are pregnant, especially in the later months, when the label warns against aspirin-containing products unless a doctor says otherwise
- Are under 18 and have the flu or chickenpox, because aspirin is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness in children and teenagers

## Is Excedrin a Good Choice for a Hangover?

It can work, but it's often not the best fit. Excedrin's caffeine and aspirin are a strong team for tension and migraine headaches, but they're also the two ingredients most likely to aggravate a hangover stomach and hangover anxiety. Its advantage over a single-ingredient pill is mostly the caffeine, and you can get that from a cup of coffee you control.

A simpler approach many people find easier on the body:

- **Water and electrolytes first.** A lot of hangover headache is driven by dehydration and poor sleep. Our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) walks through what tends to help.
- **One single-ingredient painkiller, with food, if you need it.** That makes it easier to keep track of what you've taken and stay under the limits.
- **Your normal amount of coffee, not extra.** If you drink coffee daily, skipping it can add a withdrawal headache on top of the hangover.
- **Rest.** Sleep is one of the few things that reliably helps.

Neither acetaminophen nor NSAIDs are risk-free after heavy drinking. Acetaminophen is easier on the stomach and harder on the liver. Aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen are easier on the liver and harder on the stomach and kidneys. Excedrin gives you a bit of both. Understanding [why alcohol causes headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) can help you pick the right fix, or avoid the headache in the first place.

## A Better Plan: Prevent the Headache Instead of Treating It

The most reliable way to avoid needing Excedrin after drinking is to reduce the hangover itself. The basics have the best evidence: drink less, pace yourself, eat before and while drinking, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and choose drinks lower in congeners (clear spirits tend to cause fewer hangover symptoms than dark ones). Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers each of these.

Some people also use dihydromyricetin (DHM), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. So far that is mainly rodent work, and nobody has studied DHM taken alongside Excedrin. DHM is not a painkiller, it won't cancel out the risks described in this article, and it doesn't make it safe to combine Excedrin with alcohol. If you take any medicines regularly, check our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and ask your pharmacist before adding a supplement. If you do decide to try it, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple single-ingredient option.

## The Bottom Line

Excedrin combines acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine, and each one interacts with alcohol in its own way: extra work for the liver, extra risk to the stomach lining, and a false sense of being sober. For an occasional drinker, one labeled dose the next morning, after the alcohol has cleared and with food and water, is usually reasonable. Don't take it before or during drinking, don't double up on acetaminophen or NSAIDs from other products, and don't use Excedrin PM to sleep after drinking. If you drink most days or have stomach, liver, kidney, or bleeding problems, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using it at all.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I take Excedrin after drinking alcohol?**

For most healthy adults who drink occasionally, a single labeled dose of Excedrin the morning after, once the alcohol has cleared and with food and water, is unlikely to cause serious harm. Don't take it while you're still drinking, don't exceed the label dose, and don't combine it with other acetaminophen or NSAID products. If you have 3 or more drinks most days, a history of ulcers or bleeding, liver disease, or take a blood thinner, ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

**How long after drinking can I take Excedrin?**

There's no official waiting period on the label. A sensible approach is to wait until you're sober (the body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies widely), eat something, and then take one labeled dose with a full glass of water. After a heavy night, that may mean waiting until later in the morning.

**How long after taking Excedrin can I drink alcohol?**

The acetaminophen and caffeine in a single dose are mostly cleared within several hours, but aspirin's effect on blood clotting lasts about a week because it permanently affects platelets. If you took Excedrin earlier in the day, keep any drinking light, eat with it, and don't take another dose that night. If you take Excedrin often, ask your doctor what's reasonable for you.

**Is Excedrin Migraine safe with alcohol?**

Excedrin Migraine contains the same ingredients as Excedrin Extra Strength (acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine), so the same liver, stomach bleeding, and caffeine concerns apply. Alcohol can also trigger migraines in some people, and using headache medicine too often can cause rebound headaches. If drinking regularly triggers your migraines, talk to a doctor about a migraine plan.

**Does the caffeine in Excedrin sober you up?**

No. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol level or restore your judgment and reaction time. Lab research has found that people who combine caffeine with alcohol feel less impaired than they actually are. Never use Excedrin or coffee as a reason to think you're safe to drive.

**Can I take Excedrin PM after drinking to help me sleep?**

No. Excedrin PM Headache contains diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine, instead of caffeine. Alcohol and diphenhydramine both slow the brain, and together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, and poor coordination. The label warns against using it with alcohol.

**Is Excedrin or Tylenol better for a hangover?**

Neither is risk-free after drinking. Tylenol is just acetaminophen, which is easier on the stomach but adds work for the liver. Excedrin adds aspirin, which raises the chance of stomach irritation and bleeding when combined with alcohol, plus caffeine, which can worsen jitters and nausea. Many people find a single-ingredient painkiller with food and water easier to manage. Never take both together, since both contain acetaminophen.

**Why does Excedrin's label mention 3 or more drinks a day?**

The US label carries two alcohol warnings. The acetaminophen liver warning says severe liver damage may occur in people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product. The aspirin stomach bleeding warning says the chance of bleeding is higher for the same group. If that describes your drinking, ask a doctor before using Excedrin.
